\section{Empirical strategy}\label{sec:4}\ThesisCheckNumber{section}{4}

Throughout, \(i\) indexes a child, \(h\) the household, \(c\) the DHS cluster, \(r\) the administrative region (each cluster belongs to exactly one region), and \(s\) a survey round (country). All specifications are estimated and reported as \textbf{associational}, not causal, and none is a panel, difference-in-differences, or instrumental-variables design.

\subsection{Baseline: household WASH, region fixed effects}\label{sec:4.1}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{4.1}

\[Y_{ihcr} = \alpha + \beta_W\,\text{Water}_{ih} + \beta_S\,\text{Sanitation}_{ih} + X_i'\gamma + \delta_r + \varepsilon_{ihcr}\]

Water and sanitation are \textbf{entered together} in every household specification, never one at a time. \(X_i\) is the covariate set of Section 3.4; \(\delta_r\) is a fixed effect for each of 114 pooled administrative regions, so \(\beta_W\)/\(\beta_S\) are identified from \textbf{within-region} variation only. A region contains many DHS clusters, so \(\delta_r\) still allows clusters to differ in local infrastructure or health-service access, plausibly correlated with both WASH and nutrition and not absorbed here --- motivating the cluster-fixed-effects specification below.

\subsection{Baseline: household WASH, cluster fixed effects (main specification)}\label{sec:4.2}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{4.2}

\[Y_{ihc} = \alpha_c + \beta_W\,\text{Water}_{ih} + \beta_S\,\text{Sanitation}_{ih} + X_i'\gamma + \varepsilon_{ihc}\]

\(\alpha_c\), a fixed effect for each cluster, identifies \(\beta_W\)/\(\beta_S\) from differences in household WASH \emph{among households within the same cluster}. It absorbs what every household in a cluster shares, but not differences between households within it --- wealth, education, or unobserved behaviour can still differ and keep this specification associational. Urban/rural residence is mechanically absorbed by \(\alpha_c\), since every cluster is entirely one or the other. \textbf{Wealth quintile is estimated as part of the covariate set, not omitted}: fixed effects absorb only what is constant within a cluster, and wealth varies within clusters just as WASH status does (31.6 percent of clusters vary in own-water status, 50.6 percent in own-sanitation, the variation identifying the household coefficients; a comparable check confirms wealth varies too), so there is no mechanism to remove it.

\subsection{Baseline: community WASH, region fixed effects}\label{sec:4.3}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{4.3}

\[Y_{ihcr} = \alpha + \beta_W\,\bar{C}^{\,water}_{-h,c} + \beta_S\,\bar{C}^{\,san}_{-h,c} + X_i'\gamma + \delta_r + \varepsilon_{ihcr}\]

The leave-one-out community rates (Section 3.3) are again entered together, including at Table 5.2's ``minimally adjusted'' stage. These are cluster-level, not child-level, properties, so \(\beta_W\)/\(\beta_S\) are identified mainly by comparing \emph{clusters} within the same region --- an associational estimate of a contextual exposure, not a causal spillover effect.

\textbf{Why cluster fixed effects are not used here.} The leave-one-out rate's within-cluster variation comes only from which single household is excluded from each child's own calculation --- a mechanical artefact. Its measured within-cluster standard deviation is approximately 0.007 (water) and 0.011 (sanitation), against an overall standard deviation of approximately 0.35 for both, so a cluster fixed effect would absorb nearly all genuine between-cluster variation. The historical extension (Section 4.6) differs: a real time dimension (birth-cohort variation within cluster) gives its cluster fixed effects genuine, non-mechanical variation to work with --- a design consequence of the leave-one-out construction, not an inconsistency.

\subsection{Baseline: household and community WASH, jointly; current-age heterogeneity}\label{sec:4.4}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{4.4}

\[Y_{ihcr} = \alpha + \beta_{HW}\,\text{Water}_{ih} + \beta_{HS}\,\text{Sanitation}_{ih} + \beta_{CW}\,\bar{C}^{\,water}_{-h,c} + \beta_{CS}\,\bar{C}^{\,san}_{-h,c} + X_i'\gamma + \delta_r + \varepsilon_{ihcr}\]

All four WASH terms are entered together; each coefficient is conditional on the other three. Because household and community water are fairly closely correlated, this is reported as a secondary decomposition, not a preferred model.

\[\begin{aligned}
Y_i = {}& \alpha + \beta_W\,\text{Water}_i + \beta_S\,\text{Sanitation}_i + \sum_{a \neq \text{ref}} \theta_a\,\text{AgeBand}_{ia} \\
&+ \sum_{a \neq \text{ref}} \lambda^W_a\,(\text{Water}_i \times \text{AgeBand}_{ia}) + \sum_{a \neq \text{ref}} \lambda^S_a\,(\text{Sanitation}_i \times \text{AgeBand}_{ia}) + X_i'\gamma + \text{FE} + \varepsilon_i
\end{aligned}\]

\(\text{AgeBand}_{ia}\) are six current-age bands (0--5 to 48--59 completed months, 12--23 as reference, fixed before any result was examined), replacing the continuous age control. Three joint Wald tests (\(\chi^2\)) are reported per outcome and fixed-effect structure: water-specific (5 restrictions), sanitation-specific (5), and combined (10). These test whether the survey-date WASH association differs across children's \emph{current} ages (Section 1.2) --- not a reconstruction of an older child's actual infancy exposure, and kept distinct from the historical extension's exposure-timing design.

\subsection{Inference, weighting, and the pooled estimand}\label{sec:4.5}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{4.5}

\textbf{Weighting.} Every country is given equal total weight in a pooled model of size \(N\) across \(M\) countries: \(w_i = \text{raw}_i / \sum_{j \in \text{country}(i)} \text{raw}_j\), so each country's weights sum to 1. \(\text{raw}_i\) is the sample's own native weight field (\ThesisCode{v005}-derived for the baseline, Section 3.4; \ThesisCode{PERWEIGHT} for the historical extension, Section 3.8), computed within each model's own final sample after applicable exclusions. The historical pipeline additionally multiplies by a constant that only rescales reporting with no effect on any coefficient, SE, CI, or p-value (Appendix B.1). This is an authorised, disclosed working choice, not a correction for sampling design, and does not define the pooled coefficient as any simple average.

The estimand is the single common slope of one pooled regression, not an average of separately estimated country slopes. Equal weight \emph{totals} do \textbf{not} imply equal influence: by Frisch--Waugh--Lovell logic, a country's influence on the pooled slope also depends on its residual exposure variation after controls. This thesis's own historical pooled water--HAZ estimate illustrates it: the unweighted average of the three countries' own coefficients is 0.58, while the pooled coefficient is 1.03 (Section 5.6), consistent with Kenya's residual exposure variation being roughly a third of Nigeria's and under half of Ghana's, so its imprecise, negative estimate receives little weight despite equal weight totals. Historical pooled coefficients are reported alongside their country-specific components (Tables 5.5--5.6); baseline pooled models (Sections 5.1--5.3) are not broken out by country in the same way.

\textbf{Estimator and inference.} Cluster fixed effects (household and historical models) are implemented as weighted within-cluster demeaning, equivalent to weighted least squares with cluster dummies, using the cluster-robust CRV1 sandwich with small-sample correction \(c = \frac{G}{G-1}\times\frac{N-1}{N-K}\). The two pipelines differ in reference distribution: the historical pipeline uses Student \emph{t}(\(G-1\)); the baseline pipeline (\ThesisCode{statsmodels} \autocite{Seabold2010Statsmodels}) uses the normal (z) distribution (\ThesisCode{use\_\allowbreak{}t: False}, confirmed to ten decimal places, Appendix B.1), as do the region-fixed-effects models. This thesis's primary baseline cluster-FE p-values (water--HAZ .062, sanitation--HAZ .548) are therefore normal-reference values; a more conservative convention penalising degrees of freedom for absorbed cluster dummies gives wider sensitivity p-values (.080, .574), reported as such wherever cited (Appendix B.1).

\textbf{Singleton clusters and rank.} The historical pipeline explicitly drops clusters contributing only one observation and reports the count with every model; the baseline pipeline's code contains no corresponding step, so no baseline singleton count exists --- a disclosed description gap, not an assumption it is inconsequential. Every design matrix is checked for full column rank after the fixed-effects transformation; the historical pipeline drops any fully absorbed column by name, and the baseline pipeline's only pre-specified exclusion (\ThesisCode{residence} under cluster fixed effects) is stated in Section 4.2. A well-defined, full-rank coefficient is a computational property, not a causal one.

\subsection{Historical extension: cluster fixed effects with cohort controls}\label{sec:4.6}\ThesisCheckNumber{subsection}{4.6}

\[y_{ic} = \alpha_c + \beta\,E_{ic}(w, p) + \lambda\,\text{age}_{ic} + \gamma'X_{ic} + \delta_{s,b_{ic}} + \varepsilon_{ic}\]

\(E_{ic}(w,p)\) is the annual-weighted IHME mean (product \(p\), window \(w\)) for child \(i\) in cluster \(c\), 0--100 scale (Sections 3.5--3.7); \(\beta\) is reported per 1 and per 10 points. \(\delta_{s,b}\) is a survey-specific birth-year term, each country's own birth-year effects relative to its own earliest observed year, not one pooled reference year. An early independent-reconstruction attempt used a single pooled reference year and omitted the age-in-months control, producing a materially different coefficient (1.385 vs.~the correct 1.026); a dedicated diagnostic isolates the age-in-months omission as the sole cause, the two birth-year schemes being equivalent nuisance specifications confirmed to floating-point precision (Appendix B.2). \(X_{ic}\) includes child sex, maternal age, maternal education, and marital status; wealth is excluded for the reason given in Section 3.8, not because cluster fixed effects absorb it.

\textbf{Why cluster fixed effects are appropriate here but not for community WASH (Section 4.3).} \(E_{ic}(w,p)\) varies genuinely across birth cohorts \emph{within} the same cluster --- real temporal variation, not a mechanical construction artefact. This variation, quantified as the residual exposure standard deviation after controls (Section 5.6), ranges from 0.20 to 0.88 percentage points by country and product --- modest relative to the 10-point reporting scale, which this thesis does not interpret as a typical within-cluster change. Weighting follows the same equal-country-total formula (\(M=3\)), and inference uses the Student \emph{t}(\(G-1\)) distribution the historical pipeline implements; singleton clusters are dropped and counted by its own explicit filtering step.
